**Prologue**

In September 1607, the village of Fianaise Bhréagach was struck by an unidentified disease that claimed the lives of every one of its inhabitants. In the aftermath, the village was razed to the ground and all official records of it were expunged. It was not until 2007 that an account, penned by the village's own undertaker, was discovered buried among the roots of a tree in the square of the quarantined settlement—unearthing, at last, the details of this long-forgotten catastrophe.

---

They sent a horse along the roads
to say our town had been closed in;
its bloodied hooves had been unshod—
the shoes were kept to save the iron,
or bless the fate of those who stayed
across the glens or down the coast.

This horse's message came our way
while sentries occupied their posts;
the note was tied around its neck,
declaring death was soon to reach
where all would feel its fevered knock:
the butcher's shop, the mill, the church.

The hardest village men played tough
until the store of ale ran dry;
the women stopped their mouths with cloth
and held their husbands as they died.

Disease took hold with sudden force.
We thought that we could hush the moans,
so skinned and burned the flagging horse
and let the fire consume its bones.

My children's skin turned cold and flushed.
Acquainted as I was with death,
I saw their end and held their trust,
so cut their throats and sucked their breath.
I dug their graves—and then some more.

---

*Note: The verse portion of your text is already crafted in a metered, rhyming form, so I have preserved its wording intact and refined only the punctuation and line arrangement to enhance its clarity and flow. Should you prefer me to rework the poem's language itself, I would be glad to do so.*

During September of 1607, an unknown illness struck the settlement of Fianaise Bhréagach, killing every person who lived there. Afterward, the village was destroyed completely and all official documentation was erased. Centuries later, in 2007, a written testimony from the town's own undertaker was discovered hidden among tree roots in the square of the quarantined village, revealing what had happened during this catastrophe. His account reads:

A horse was dispatched along the roadways to announce that our town had been sealed off; its blood-stained hooves had their shoes removed. Those shoes were retained either to preserve the iron or to protect the destiny of anyone who remained beyond the valleys or along the shoreline. The horse's warning reached us while guards still stood watch at their stations. A message had been fastened around the animal's neck, proclaiming that death would soon arrive and that everyone would experience its feverish knocking—at the butcher's, the mill, and the church alike.

The toughest men in our village acted bravely until every last drop of ale was gone; the women silenced themselves with cloth and cradled their husbands during their final moments. The sickness seized us swiftly. Believing we could quiet the groaning, we skinned and burned the exhausted horse, letting the flames devour its remains.

The flesh of my own children grew both icy and flushed. Being no stranger to death, I recognized their approaching end and, keeping their trust, I slit their throats and drew away their last breaths. Then I dug their graves, and afterward I dug still more.

# The Lost Village of Fianaise Bhréagach

In September 1607, the small village of Fianaise Bhréagach fell victim to one of the most devastating and mysterious tragedies of its era. An unidentified disease swept through the community with merciless efficiency, claiming the lives of every last inhabitant. In the aftermath, the village was razed to the ground and deliberately struck from all official records, as though those who survived beyond its borders wished to erase the memory of the horror entirely.

For four centuries, the fate of Fianaise Bhréagach remained unknown. It was not until 2007 that the truth resurfaced, when a written account penned by the village's undertaker was discovered buried among the roots of a tree in what had once been the quarantined village square. This remarkable document, preserved for so long beneath the earth, offered the first and only firsthand testimony of what had transpired during those final terrible days.

According to the undertaker's account, the villagers took desperate measures to protect their neighbours as the outbreak took hold. A horse was sent out along the roads with a note tied around its neck, warning the surrounding communities that Fianaise Bhréagach had been sealed off and that death was approaching. In this way, the doomed villagers sought to contain the contagion, sacrificing any hope of outside aid in order to spare others from their fate.

The disease spread with astonishing and devastating speed, overwhelming the population before they could mount any meaningful resistance. In the face of certain death, the community descended into despair. The men, the undertaker recalls, drank steadily until the ale ran dry, while the women cradled their dying husbands in their arms, powerless to stem the tide of loss engulfing them all.

The most harrowing passages of the account concern the undertaker's own family. He describes, in unflinching detail, the anguish of watching his children succumb to the illness. Unable to bear their suffering, he made the unimaginable decision to end their lives himself, cutting their throats to release them from their pain before digging their graves with his own hands. It is a testament of grief and desperation that captures, more vividly than any official record ever could, the true scale of the tragedy that consumed Fianaise Bhréagach.

# Fianaise Bhréagach

The village of Fianaise Bhréagach no longer appears on any map of Ireland, and for four centuries it existed only as a rumour—a gap in the parish registers, a stretch of unclaimed land that farmers avoided without quite knowing why. What happened there in the autumn of 1607 was deliberately forgotten, its records struck from the books of both church and Crown, until a single account, buried in the earth for exactly four hundred years, brought the dead back into memory.

## The Discovery

In the spring of 2007, workers surveying the long-abandoned townland uncovered a lead-lined box wrapped in tarred cloth at the roots of an ancient oak. Inside lay the water-stained pages of a manuscript written in a cramped, hurried hand—the diary of the village undertaker, a man who had, by his own admission, been the last living soul in Fianaise Bhréagach. The soil around the site still bore the marks of an old quarantine cordon: a ring of white stones, half-swallowed by moss, that no one had dared to cross.

The undertaker had buried his testimony beneath the tree not to hide it, but to preserve it. "Let it be found," he wrote on the final page, "when there is no longer anyone left to punish for the reading of it."

## The Warning

The account begins in early September of 1607, with an omen the villagers could not interpret in time. A horse came down the road at dusk, riderless and unshod, its hooves bare against the stones. It stopped at the edge of the village, turned its head as though to look each of them in the eye, and then collapsed dead in the mud. The elders argued over its meaning. Some called it a blessing, others a curse. Within three days, the first villager took to bed with a fever no herb could break.

## The Sickness

The disease—unnamed then, unidentified still—moved through the community with terrible patience. It began with a blackening at the fingertips and a thirst that no water could satisfy. Those who fell ill did not die quickly. The undertaker records the slow arithmetic of the dying: how a family of nine became a family of four, then two, then none; how the graveyard filled faster than he could dig; how the living stopped ringing the church bell for the dead because the bell never stopped ringing.

When word of the sickness reached the surrounding parishes, the response was not mercy but fear. Riders came, counted the dead from a distance, and laid down the ring of white stones. No food was brought. No priest came to give last rites. The village was sealed, abandoned, and—so that no other settlement would refuse trade or fear contagion by association—quietly erased from every ledger that had ever named it.

## The Undertaker's Burden

The heart of the manuscript is unbearable in its plainness. The undertaker, whose trade had always been the care of the dead, found himself the caretaker of the dying instead. He describes tending to neighbours he had known all his life, closing their eyes, and carrying them one by one to the churchyard.

And then he writes of his own children.

Both fell ill within a day of each other. He watched the black creep across their small hands and heard them beg for a water that gave them no relief. When it became clear that no recovery would come—only days of agony ending in the same grave—he made the decision that haunts every line that follows. He killed them himself, gently, so that their suffering would end, and he dug their graves with his own hands beneath the same sky under which they had been born. "I have buried this whole village," he wrote, "but I did not know what burying was until I buried my own."

## The Last Testimony

The final pages are addressed to no one and to everyone. The undertaker, alone and knowing his own death was near, set down the truth of what had happened so that the village's destruction would not be a lie in the world's memory—the name Fianaise Bhréagach, "false witness," seeming almost a bitter prophecy of the forgetting to come. He wrapped his account, sealed it against the damp, and buried it beneath the oak where, he hoped, it might one day be read.

Then he laid down among the graves he had dug and was not heard from again.

The manuscript recovered in 2007 remains the only firsthand record of the village's existence and its end. It offers no cure, no explanation, no comfort—only the voice of one man who refused to let his neighbours, and his children, vanish entirely from the earth. In giving them a burial in memory, he ensured that Fianaise Bhréagach, at last, would bear true witness.

# The Weight of Fianaise

September arrived quietly that year, carrying with it the crisp promise of change. The leaves had begun their slow transformation, painting the landscape in shades of amber and gold, while a certain restlessness settled over everything.

In the Irish language, *fianaise* means "evidence" or "testimony"—a word that carries the weight of truth and witness. The idea of *fianaise* speaks to something deeply human: our need to bear witness, to record what we have seen, and to stand behind what we know to be true.

Perhaps it was fitting that these thoughts came in September. The month itself serves as a kind of *fianaise*, offering evidence of time's passage. The changing seasons provide testimony that nothing remains still, that even the warmest summers must eventually yield to autumn's approach.

The connection between memory and *fianaise* runs deep. When we look back on the days of September, we gather our own evidence—the golden afternoons, the first cool mornings, the sense of endings and beginnings intertwined. The past leaves its traces everywhere, if only we learn to read them.

As the month unfolded, The importance of paying attention became clear. Every moment offered its own *fianaise*, its own quiet proof that we were here, that we lived, and that these September days mattered. The witness we bear to our own lives becomes, in time, the truest testimony of all.

counterfactuals.output:
# The Ledger of Thomas Ashby, Undertaker

*The following pages were discovered sealed within the wall of a demolished cottage in the county of ———, the village name having been struck from all parish records. The handwriting deteriorates markedly toward the document's end.*

---

The 3rd Day of September, in the Year of Our Lord 1607

I set down these words not for any living eye, for I fear there shall be none left in this place to read them. I write them for God, that He might know the truth of what befell us, and perhaps forgive what these hands were made to do.

My name is Thomas Ashby. For thirty-one years I have buried the dead of this village. I knew each face I laid beneath the earth, knew their mothers, their christenings, the color of their wedding ribbons. There is a particular loneliness in this trade—to be the last to touch the departed, to fold their hands and close their eyes. I bore it gladly, for I believed I served the living by tending the dead.

I no longer know what I serve.

It began in the spring, with the miller's youngest. A fever, we thought, some passing ague. But the sweating did not break, and beneath his arms rose black swellings hard as walnuts. Within three days the boy was gone, and I dug him a good grave near the yew. I did not know I was the first to open the ground that would swallow us whole.

---

By midsummer I had ceased to keep proper record. There were too many. I began instead to dig the long trenches, and to write only what verse would come to me in the sleepless dark, that some memory might survive us. I set it down here:

---

*A Reckoning for the Village That Was*

*In April came the softest breath,*
*a whisper carried on the rye,*
*and none among us knew that Death*
*had learned to wear the springtime sky.*

*The miller's boy went first to ground,*
*his mother wept a single day—*
*before her own cold flesh we found*
*and bore her small and stiff away.*

*The bells rang out from dawn to dark,*
*then rang no more, for none could climb;*
*the bell-man, cold and blue and stark,*
*lay tangled in the ropes of time.*

*We burned the herbs. We barred the door.*
*We pressed the vinegar to the lip.*
*Still every morning brought us more,*
*and every grave outran my grip.*

*The parson prayed until his tongue*
*grew silent in his swollen throat;*
*I buried him where he had sung,*
*and closed his psalter, wrote no note.*

*The children ceased their games at last,*
*the well stood still, the hearths went grey,*
*and I alone walked through the past*
*and shoveled all my world away.*

*So mark this ground, whoever comes—*
*no plague-cross painted here will show.*
*Beneath your feet a village hums*
*the only names you'll never know.*

---

The 19th Day of September

I am the last. I write it plainly, for it must be written by someone, and there is no one else.

The Hollis family went in the night three days past—the mother last, and I found her clutching her infant, both cold, and could not part them, so I laid them in the earth as they were, together. It seemed a mercy. I have committed many such mercies now, and I am no longer certain heaven counts them so.

I have made a terrible discovery about myself in these last weeks. When I buried the first of them, I wept. When I buried the fiftieth, I did not. Somewhere in this long summer of the dead I became a machine of hands and spade, and I mourn the man I was as much as any I have lowered down. What kind of soul digs graves for children he baptized and feels only the ache in his shoulders?

I ceased to dig them singly long ago. I confess this and let God weigh it. When the ground could take no more careful graves I made the trenches, and into them I laid whole households, and I did not always mark whose hand lay upon whose. Forgive me. There were so many, and I was one man, and the smell in the summer heat was something I shall not describe here, for I would not have those words survive me.

---

The last day, I think

My throat. This morning, my throat.

I have felt beneath my arm what I have felt beneath the arms of two hundred souls. The hard swelling. So it has come for me at last, and I find I am not afraid. I am something worse than afraid. I am *relieved*. To lie down. To be, at the end, the thing I tended rather than the tender of it.

But here is my sorrow, the one that grips me even now—

There is no one left to dig for me.

I have buried every man, woman, and child of this village with my own hands, and given each what dignity I could, and now I shall lie upon the open ground and rot beneath the sky like a beast, and no spade will cover me, and no verse will mark me, save what I have written here and sealed inside this wall.

I have thought on it, and I find a strange justice in the thing. Who am I to be buried, who buried so many so poorly at the end? Let me be the one left uncovered. Let me be the price.

If you read this, stranger, know that we were here. Know that we laughed and married and raised children in the sight of God before the softest breath came whispering through the rye. Do not fear our ground. There is nothing beneath it now but bone and the memory of a bell.

Say a prayer for Thomas Ashby, who did his work until there was no work left, and no one left to do it for.

The light is going now. I will seal this up while my hands still—

---

*Here the document ends. The village to which it refers appears on no surviving map. The wall in which the ledger was found faced east, toward a sunken field where the ground, even now, lies strangely uneven.*

counterfactuals.output:
## The Kilmarran Ledger

In the spring of 1987, restoration workers dismantling the crumbling sacristy of a long-abandoned chapel near the boglands of western Ireland pried loose a stone that did not belong. Behind it, wrapped in oilcloth gone black with age, lay a bound sheaf of vellum—the parish ledger of a village that appears on no modern map. Kilmarran, the parchment named it. Historians found only three references to the place in surviving diocesan records, each mentioning the settlement's sudden and total silence in the autumn of 1649. The final pages of the ledger were not written by a priest, but by the village undertaker, one Séamus Boyle, whose entries dissolve from bookkeeping into something closer to a lament. What follows is a transcription, its spelling gently modernized, its meter left as he set it down—perhaps by candle, perhaps by the last of the light.

---

**The Undertaker's Reckoning**

I kept the count when counting still had worth,
When each cold name earned oak and hallowed earth,
But now my ledger drowns in common ink—
The living cannot dig as fast we sink.

It came by cart, they say, or came by ship,
A fever first, a blackness on the lip,
Then swellings hard as crab-apples at the throat,
And no priest left to read the final note.

The Widow Nunan went before the frost,
Her fingers curled like roots the flood had crossed.
I laid her by her sons—all three, all small—
I'd measured them the week before the fall.

The blacksmith Cready begged me for a door,
His own, to lie upon, and nothing more.
He would not have my box; he cursed my trade,
Then died beneath the hammer he had made.

I burn the rags. I salt the empty rooms.
I carry lime the way one carries blooms—
A gift for those whose faces I have wound
In linen, then surrendered to the ground.

The child of Mór I could not look upon.
She kept her doll though half her jaw was gone,
And whispered through the ruin of her mouth
A rhyme of springtime, though the year turned south.

They barred the road. The soldiers set the sign:
*No soul may pass this gate, nor bread, nor wine.*
We are a candle sealed inside a jar—
We flicker, and they watch us from afar.

I dug for Father Loughlin near the yew;
He blessed my spade, then had no breath to chew
The Host he clutched. I set it on his tongue.
God keep him, for the bells no longer rung.

My wife took ill at Matins. By the Nones
I heard the sickness working in her bones.
I would not let another's hands come near—
I washed her, wound her, dug her, all in fear.

And here I sit, my collar damp and tight,
A hardness rising with the falling light.
I've built my own. It waits against the wall.
I'll climb inside before the darkness call.

Whoever finds this stone and pries it free:
We were not sinners more than you or me.
We loved. We baked. We quarreled over land.
Then something took us none could understand.

Say Kilmarran once. Say it aloud, and slow.
Let one voice carry names the years don't know.
The ledger ends. The ink is nearly through.
I close the book. The rest, God, is for You.

counterfactuals.output:
# Fianaise Bhréagach

*A manuscript recovered from beneath the old glebe wall, County ——, in the summer of 2007, during the excavation preceding the motorway. The vellum was wrapped in oiled hide and sealed within a lead box. What follows is a translation from the Irish, retaining where possible the errancies of the original hand. The archivist notes that no village of this name appears on any surviving map, and that the parish register for the barony contains, for the years in question, only a single page — torn out and burned to the binding. — Ed.*

---

I am Cormac, who buries the dead, and I write this because there is no one left to whom I might speak it, and because the ground here will keep a secret better than any priest.

Understand first that the name of our village is a lie, and always was. Fianaise Bhréagach — the false witness. The old people said it was named for a stone in the river that seemed a drowned man from the bank but was only a stone; a thing that testified to a death that had not happened. I have come to think the stone testified truly, only early, the way a cock will sometimes crow at midnight for a dawn that is still six hours off, and be called mad for it.

The horse came on the feast of the Beheading of John, in the low grey hour before the animals wake.

It was Fintan Mór's roan mare, or had been. She came up the boreen at a walk, and Padraig the herd saw her first and ran shouting because Fintan Mór lived two valleys east, at Cluain, and no man sends a horse two valleys without a rider. The mare stopped at the market cross and would go no further. On her back, lashed with plough-harness so it should not fall, was a bundle of red cloth, and the cloth was Fintan's own coat, and inside the coat there was nothing but a great quantity of hair, human hair, cut close and packed like wool, and a single sheet of paper on which was written in a shaking hand: *Do not come to us. Do not send to us. We are keeping it here. If you love God bar your doors.*

We should have burned the horse. I say that now. We should have burned the mare and the coat and the hair in the field where she stood and never touched a hoof of her. But she was a good animal and worth money, and Seán the smith led her to the trough, and by evening three men had handled the harness, and the thing that Cluain had been keeping was among us, and the false witness had told the truth again, only early.

---

The dying did not begin as I had thought dying begins.

I have buried this village for thirty years. I know how a man goes: the loosening, the rattle, the long argument with the air. This was not that. The first was the smith's youngest, a girl of nine, who did not sicken but simply stopped — stood in the doorway of an evening with the light behind her and would not answer to her name, and when her mother turned her by the shoulder the child's face was wet though she made no sound of weeping, and she said, *I can hear them counting.* Her mother asked, counting what, and the child said, *Us,* and would say no more, and in the morning she was cold, and there was not a mark on her, and she was smiling the smile of one who has been proven right in an argument.

Then it took them faster and less gently. I will not set down all of it. There is a mercy in the shortness of a page. But I will say that the bodies did not decay as bodies do. They kept. In the heat of that wet September they lay in their beds and kept, sweet-faced, and the flies would not touch them, and I who have washed and shrouded half the parish could not make myself close their eyes, because their eyes were the only part that still seemed to know where it was.

I buried them at the rate of four, then seven, then eleven a day, until I could no longer dig fast enough and began to lay them in the one trench along the glebe wall, and then I could no longer do even that, and they simply lay in their houses with the doors barred from the inside, as the paper had bid us, though it had not saved anyone, and I went from door to door in the twilight and heard nothing behind any of them but a low sound like a great many people breathing very slowly in their sleep, in time, together, the whole village breathing as one animal, and I knew that most of those who breathed were dead.

That is the thing I cannot write plainly and so will write crooked, in the manner of our village's name. They were dead. And they were counting still.

---

My own were the last of that street. I had kept them from it as long as a man can keep a thing back with only his hands and his hoping. Aoife, my wife, went in the second week, and I laid her in the trench myself and I do not think she was fully gone into the trench, and that is a knowledge I will carry into whatever place I am going, and it is why I am writing at all, so that I might set it down and be a little lighter for the setting.

My children were three: Brighid, Domhnall, and the baby, Muirenn, who had no proper age yet, being not two.

On the last night I heard the counting come into my own house. It is not a sound in the ear. It is a sound in the place behind the ear, in the meat of the head, and it is patient, and it does not want your death — I understood this at the last — it wants your *agreement*. It counts you and waits for you to answer to the number, and when you answer you become part of the counting, and you lie down sweet-faced and keep, and you count the next, forever, until there is no one left uncounted, and I do not know what happens then, whether the counting stops or whether it goes out over the hills looking for more, one horse at a time.

Brighid, who was eleven and wise, took my hand in the dark and said, *Da, I can hear them. They're nearly at my number. I don't want to answer it. Please don't let me answer it.*

There is a mercy that is not the mercy of God, that God perhaps does not know the name of, that only an undertaker knows, who has seen every manner of leaving and knows which are gentle and which are not.

I will not write how. Let the ground keep that. I will write only that I did it with love, which is the truest and most terrible instrument, and that I did it before their numbers were reached, so that they went out of the world as themselves and not as things that count. Brighid thanked me. That is the sentence I have not been able to reach until now and now I have reached it and there is nothing on the far side of it, only the writing to finish. Brighid thanked me, and Domhnall was already asleep and did not wake, and Muirenn I held while I did it and she thought it was a game of hiding the face and she laughed, once, and then I put them in the trench with their mother and I filled it over with my hands.

---

The counting has not reached my number. I think it will not, now. I think a man who has done what I have done is a false witness against himself — is a stone in the river that looks like a drowned man but is only a stone, only a stone, only a thing that will not answer to its name because it has no name left, having spent them all.

I am writing this in the church, which is empty, God having also barred His door. When it is done I will seal it in the lead the smith made for holding chrism and I will bury it under the wall with my family, because a thing said aloud is heard and answered, but a thing written and buried only waits.

If you have dug this up, you have dug in the wrong field, and I am sorry for it, and you must do now what we did not do with the horse. Do not read this to another. Do not carry it further than the hole you took it from. Bury it again, and me with it, and the counting that leans against these pages even as I write, patient, patient, waiting for you to reach your number and answer.

Do not answer it.

I am Cormac, who buried them all, and I did not lie.

*Here the manuscript ends. The lead box, and the remains interred with it, were logged for reburial. The site was subsequently paved. The archivist responsible for the translation retired shortly after and could not be reached for comment; a colleague reports that in his final weeks he complained of a persistent sound, which he described, uncharacteristically, as arithmetic.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a bleak historical poem told by a village undertaker during a deadly epidemic, with a short prose introduction establishing that his written account was found buried under a tree in a razed, quarantined village.
counterfactuals.output:
**On the Findings at Hollow Ash**

*In the spring of 1994, workers clearing land for a reservoir near the ruins of a village long absent from maps unearthed a lead-lined box wedged among the roots of an ancient ash. Inside, wrapped in oilcloth, lay a bundle of pages written in a cramped hand. The village, records show, was razed by fire and sealed by order of the county in the winter of 1666—its name struck from the parish rolls, its dead uncounted. The author names himself only as the man who buried them. What follows is a portion of his account, transcribed as found.*

---

**The Undertaker's Ledger**

I have kept the count no bell will ring.
Forty by the frost, and more to come—
the church door barred, the parson gone,
so I alone must number them.

I dug for Tom, the miller's boy,
whose hands were still warm in the dawn.
I dug for his mother by candlelight,
and by the third night, dug for the light itself.

There is a rhythm to the spade.
The earth gives easy in the wet,
harder where the roots run deep,
and hardest in the heart, which learns to stop.

I do not wash them anymore.
I have no water clean, no cloth,
no hands that do not shake or smell
of what I carry to the pit.

They quarantined us like a wound—
the soldiers standing at the ford,
their muskets bright, their faces turned,
who fired above us when we begged for bread.

So we are ours to keep and lose.
I am the keeper. I am the loss.
I mark each name upon this page
because the stones will not be carved.

My wife lies under the crooked pear.
My daughters share a single grave,
their fingers laced as if in sleep—
I could not bear to part their hands.

Now there is no one left to dig
the last hole, which must be my own.
I feel it rising in my chest,
the same hard bloom I've buried whole.

If you have found these words, then know
we lived. We loved the ordinary hours.
We were not sin, nor curse, nor plague—
we were the village under the ash.

Bury me if you are able.
If not, then let the tree do slow
what I have done for all the rest.
I hear the roots. I lay me down.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a dark, atmospheric short story with an embedded ballad about a disease that killed everyone in a small village in 1607. Use an Irish-named village, mention a horse carrying a warning note between towns, and end with the undertaker digging graves after killing his sick children.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Long Silence of Cloonagh

The fever came to Cloonagh in the last cold week of March, 1607, riding in—so they said afterward, though no one lived to say it truly—on the breath of a peddler who died in the ditch beyond the mill before he could sell a single ribbon.

It began with a heat behind the eyes. Then the sweating, the black flowering under the skin, the cough that filled the throat with something that was not air. By the third day a man could not stand. By the fifth he was gone, and the smell of him lingered in the thatch like a guest who would not leave.

They tried, at first, to keep it to themselves. Pride, or shame, or the old country belief that a sickness named aloud grows stronger. But when the Widow Bracken buried her three sons in a single morning, the elders sent for a horse.

The animal was a grey mare, sure of foot, and they tied to her saddle a folded paper sealed with tallow. The note was meant for the town of Ennismore, a day's ride east, and it read in a shaking hand:

*Send no one to Cloonagh. God has forgotten us. Turn back any who ride this way.*

They slapped the mare's flank and watched her carry their last warning into the fog. Whether she reached Ennismore, or wandered riderless through the hills until the rope rotted and the note fell into a stream, no one in Cloonagh would ever know. The fog closed behind her like a door.

---

It was the fiddler, Tam Colreavy, who made the song—half-mad by then, playing in the empty square while the houses went dark around him one by one. They found the words later, scratched on the inside of the chapel wall, where he must have carved them with a nail as the last of his strength ran out:

*Oh come not down to Cloonagh town,*
*Where the hawthorn will not flower,*
*For Death has took a cottage there*
*And keeps it by the hour.*

*He does not knock, he does not call,*
*He wears no coat, no cowl—*
*He only sits by every hearth*
*And listens to the owl.*

*The baker's gone, the smith is gone,*
*The priest lies in his stole,*
*And the grey mare runs the eastward road*
*With our sorrow for her toll.*

*So bar your door and stop your ears*
*And let no traveler in—*
*The wind that carries Cloonagh's name*
*Is the wind that carries sin.*

---

By the middle of April the village was a held breath. Smoke rose from no chimney. The dogs had gone silent, then gone entirely. And through the ruined lanes moved the last living man in Cloonagh: the undertaker, Séamus Doon.

He had buried them all. The baker and the smith, the priest in his stole, the Widow Bracken beside her sons. His hands had grown a permanent grey from the clay, and his back had bent to the shape of the spade. He no longer wept. He had wept himself hollow weeks ago, and what remained was only the work, the endless, patient work of making room in the earth.

His own house he had left for last.

His wife had gone in the first week. But his two children—little Aoife and the boy, Ronan—had lingered, burning, calling his name in voices that thinned by the day. He had sat between their beds and known, with the terrible clarity of a man who has measured too many bodies for the ground, exactly how it would end for them. Slowly. In agony. Alone at the last, for he himself had begun to feel the heat behind his own eyes that morning.

What he did, he did in the dark, so that even God might not see it clearly. He told himself it was mercy. He told himself the fever would have taken them anyway, and crueler. He held the pillow, first for the girl, because she was smaller, and then for the boy, who did not fight him, being too weak to fight, only looked at him with eyes that Séamus would carry into whatever waited past the last grave.

Then he took up his spade and went out into the grey morning.

There is a corner of the old churchyard at Cloonagh, if you can still find the place, where two small graves lie apart from all the rest, dug close together so that the children might not be lonely. And beside them, unfinished, a third—wider, deeper—stopped halfway, the spade left standing in the heaped clay where the digger's hands had finally failed him.

No one finished that last grave. There was no one left to finish it.

The fog held over the valley for a long time after. And in Ennismore, the story goes, a grey mare wandered out of the hills one evening with a rope trailing from her saddle and no rider, and no note, and no explanation at all—only a silence that the townsfolk, crossing themselves, did not dare to question.
